chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter III
paragraphs: Next morning, having said goodbye to no one but the count and without waiting for the ladies to appear, Prince Andrew set off for home.

It was already the beginning of June when, on his return journey, he drove into the birch forest where the gnarled old oak had made such a strange and memorable impression on him. In the forest the harness bells sounded even more muffled than they had six weeks before, for now everything was thick, shady, and dense. The young firs scattered through the forest no longer clashed with the general beauty but, blending in with the mood around them, were delicately green with fluffy new shoots.

The whole day had been hot. Somewhere a storm was gathering, but only a small cloud had sprinkled a few raindrops on the road and the juicy leaves. The left side of the forest was dark in shadow; the right side sparkled in the sunlight, wet and glistening and barely stirred by the breeze. Everything was in bloom, the nightingales trilled, and their songs echoed now near, now far away.

"Yes — it was here in this forest, with that oak I agreed with," thought Prince Andrew. "But where is it?" he wondered again, looking to the left side of the road, and without recognizing it, he gazed in admiration at the very oak he had been looking for. The old oak, completely transformed, spread a canopy of rich, dark-green foliage and stood swaying gently, almost trembling, in the rays of the evening sun. Neither gnarled fingers nor old scars nor old doubts and sorrows were anywhere in evidence. Through the tough, century-old bark — even where there were no branches — leaves had sprouted, so fresh and vigorous it was hard to believe the old veteran could have produced them.

"Yes, it is the same oak," thought Prince Andrew, and all at once he was seized by an unreasoning springtime feeling of joy and renewal. All the best moments of his life suddenly rose to his memory. Austerlitz with the vast heavens, his wife's dead, reproachful face, Pierre at the ferry, that girl thrilled by the beauty of the night, and that night itself, and the moon — all of it rushed suddenly into his mind.

"No, life is not over at thirty-one!" Prince Andrew suddenly decided, finally and irrevocably. "It's not enough for me to know what I have inside me — everyone must know it: Pierre, and that young girl who wanted to fly into the sky — everyone must know me, so that my life is not lived for myself alone, apart from everyone else, but so that it is reflected in them all, and they and I may live in harmony!"

On reaching home, Prince Andrew decided to go to Petersburg that autumn and found all sorts of reasons to justify this decision. A whole series of sensible, logical arguments showing that it was essential to go — and even to re-enter the service — kept springing up in his mind. He could not now understand how he had ever doubted the necessity of taking an active part in life, just as a month ago he hadn't understood how the idea of leaving the country could enter his head. It now seemed clear that all his experience of life would be senselessly wasted unless he put it to some use and played an active role again. He didn't even remember how, on the strength of similar flimsy logic, it had previously seemed obvious that he'd be debasing himself if he allowed himself — after the lessons life had taught him — to believe again in the possibility of being useful, and in the possibility of happiness or love. Now reason pointed in exactly the opposite direction. After that trip to Ryazan he found country life dull; his old pursuits no longer interested him, and often, sitting alone in his study, he would get up, go to the mirror, and stare at his own face for a long time. Then he would turn away to look at the portrait of his dead Lise, who, with her hair curled a la grecque, gazed out of the gilt frame tenderly and cheerfully. She no longer spoke those terrible words to him but simply looked at him — merrily, curiously, and questioningly. And Prince Andrew, clasping his hands behind his back, would pace the room for ages, now frowning, now smiling, as he pondered those irrational, inexpressible thoughts — secret as a crime — that altered his entire life and were connected with Pierre, with fame, with the girl at the window, the oak, and woman's beauty and love. And if anyone came into his room at such moments, he was particularly cold, stern, and above all unpleasantly logical.
"My dear," Princess Mary would say, entering at such a moment, "little Nicholas can't go out today — it's very cold."

"If it were hot," Prince Andrew would reply at such times very drily to his sister, "he could go out in his smock. But since it's cold, he must wear warm clothes, which were designed for that purpose. That is the logical consequence of it being cold — not that a child who needs fresh air should be kept indoors." He would add this with exaggerated logic, as if punishing someone for those secret, illogical emotions stirring within him.
At such moments Princess Mary would think how intellectual work dries men up.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: Prince Andrew arrived in Petersburg in August 1809. It was the time when the young Speransky was at the peak of his fame and his reforms were being pushed forward with the greatest energy. That same August, the Emperor was thrown from his carriage, injured his leg, and spent three weeks at Peterhof, receiving Speransky every day and no one else. At that time the two famous decrees were being prepared that so agitated society — abolishing court ranks and requiring examinations for the grades of Collegiate Assessor and State Councilor — and not just these, but a whole state constitution intended to transform the existing system of government in Russia: legal, administrative, and financial, from the Council of State down to the district courts. Now those vague liberal dreams with which Emperor Alexander had ascended the throne, and which he had tried to realize with the help of his associates Czartoryski, Novosiltsev, Kochubey, and Strogonov — whom he himself jokingly called his Comite de salut public — were taking concrete shape.

Now all these men had been replaced by Speransky on the civilian side and Arakcheev on the military. Soon after his arrival, Prince Andrew — as a gentleman of the chamber — presented himself at court and at a levee. The Emperor, though he saw him twice, did not favor him with a single word. It had always seemed to Prince Andrew that he was antipathetic to the Emperor, that the sovereign disliked his face and personality — and in the cold, distant glance Alexander gave him, he found further confirmation. The courtiers explained the Emperor's neglect as displeasure at Bolkonski's not having served since 1805.

"I know perfectly well that one can't help one's sympathies and antipathies," thought Prince Andrew, "so there's no point presenting my proposal for army reform to the Emperor personally. The project will speak for itself."

He mentioned what he had written to an old field marshal who was a friend of his father's. The field marshal gave him an appointment, received him graciously, and promised to inform the Emperor. A few days later, Prince Andrew received notice that he was to see the Minister of War, Count Arakcheev.
On the appointed day, Prince Andrew entered Count Arakcheev's waiting room at nine in the morning.
He didn't know Arakcheev personally, had never seen him, and everything he'd heard about the man inspired little respect.

"He is the Minister of War, a man trusted by the Emperor — I needn't concern myself with his personal qualities. He's been asked to review my project, and he alone can get it approved," thought Prince Andrew as he waited among various important and unimportant people in Arakcheev's anteroom.

During his time as an aide-de-camp, Prince Andrew had seen the waiting rooms of many powerful men and knew the different types well. Arakcheev's anteroom had a very distinctive character. The faces of the minor petitioners showed embarrassment and servility; the faces of those of higher rank wore a shared expression of unease, masked by an air of indifference and ironic self-mockery directed at themselves, their situation, and the person they were waiting to see. Some paced thoughtfully; others whispered and laughed. Prince Andrew heard the nickname "Sila Andreevich" and the words "Uncle will give it to us hot" — in reference to Arakcheev. One general, an important person, was clearly offended at having to wait so long and sat crossing and uncrossing his legs, smiling contemptuously to himself.

But the moment the door opened, every face showed one expression only: fear. Prince Andrew asked the duty adjutant a second time to announce him, but received an ironic look and was told his turn would come. After several others had been shown in and out of the minister's office, an officer entered whose humiliated, frightened manner struck Prince Andrew. This man's audience lasted a long time. Then suddenly a harsh, grating voice was heard from behind the door, and the officer — pale-faced and trembling — came out through the waiting room, clutching his head.
After this, Prince Andrew was led to the door, and the duty officer whispered: "To the right, by the window."

Prince Andrew entered a plain, tidy room and saw at the table a man of about forty with a long torso, a long close-cropped head, deep wrinkles, scowling brows above dull greenish-hazel eyes, and a large, overhanging red nose. Arakcheev turned his head toward him without actually looking at him.
"What is your petition?" asked Arakcheev.
"I am not petitioning, your excellency," Prince Andrew replied quietly.
Arakcheev's eyes turned toward him.
"Sit down," he said. "Prince Bolkonski?"
"I'm not petitioning for anything. His Majesty the Emperor has been pleased to send your excellency a project I submitted..."

"You see, my dear sir, I have read your project," Arakcheev interrupted, beginning amiably enough but then — again without looking at Prince Andrew — gradually lapsing into a tone of grumbling contempt. "You are proposing new military laws? There are plenty of laws already, but no one to enforce the old ones. Nowadays everyone designs laws — it's easier to write than to act."
"I came at His Majesty the Emperor's wish to learn how your excellency proposes to deal with the memorandum I submitted," said Prince Andrew politely.

"I have written my comments on your memorandum and forwarded it to the committee. I do not approve of it," said Arakcheev, standing up and taking a paper from his desk. "Here!" And he handed it to Prince Andrew.

Scrawled across the paper in pencil, without capitals, misspelled, and without punctuation, was: "unsoundly constructed because resembles an imitation of the french military code and from the articles of war needlessly deviating."
"To which committee has the memorandum been referred?" asked Prince Andrew.
"To the Committee on Army Regulations. And I have recommended that your honor be appointed a member — but without salary."
Prince Andrew smiled.
"I don't want one."
"A member without salary," repeated Arakcheev. "I have the honor... Well! Call the next one! Who else is there?" he shouted, bowing Prince Andrew out.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter V
paragraphs: While waiting for his committee appointment, Prince Andrew looked up his old acquaintances, particularly those he knew to be in power and whose help he might need. In Petersburg he now felt what he had felt on the eve of battle: a troubled curiosity, an irresistible pull toward the ruling circles where the future — on which the fate of millions depended — was being shaped. From the irritation of older officials, the curiosity of outsiders, the discretion of insiders, the hurry and preoccupation of everyone, and the countless committees and commissions he heard about daily, he sensed that here in Petersburg in 1809, a vast civic battle was being prepared — one whose commander in chief was a mysterious figure he didn't know but who was said to be a genius: Speransky. And this reform movement, which Prince Andrew understood only vaguely, with Speransky as its chief driver, began to interest him so intensely that the question of army regulations quickly receded to second place in his mind.

Prince Andrew was ideally positioned to gain entry to the highest and most varied Petersburg circles. The reforming party welcomed and courted him — first because he was reputed to be clever and exceptionally well-read, and second because by freeing his serfs he had earned a reputation as a liberal. The old guard, who disapproved of the innovations, turned to him expecting sympathy, simply because he was his father's son. Fashionable society welcomed him gladly because he was rich, distinguished, a good match, and almost a newcomer with a halo of romance from his supposed death and the tragic loss of his wife. Besides all this, the general view of everyone who had known him before was that he had greatly improved over the past five years — softened, become more mature, lost his old affectation, pride, and contemptuous irony, and gained the calm that comes with age. People talked about him, were interested in him, and wanted to meet him.

The day after his interview with Arakcheev, Prince Andrew spent the evening at Count Kochubey's. He told the count about his meeting with "Sila Andreevich" — Kochubey used that nickname with the same vague irony Prince Andrew had noticed in the War Minister's waiting room.
"My dear friend, even in this matter you can't get by without Michael Mikhailovich Speransky. He manages everything. I'll speak to him. He's promised to come this evening."
"What does Speransky have to do with army regulations?" asked Prince Andrew.
Kochubey shook his head with a knowing smile, as if surprised by Bolkonski's naivety.
"We were talking about you with him just the other day," Kochubey continued, "and about your freed serfs."
"Oh, so it's you, Prince, who've freed your serfs?" said an old man of Catherine's era, turning contemptuously toward Bolkonski.
"It was a small estate that brought in no income," replied Prince Andrew, trying to downplay his action so as not to needlessly irritate the old man.
"Afraid of being late..." said the old man, glancing at Kochubey.

"There's one thing I don't understand," he went on. "Who will plow the land if they're set free? It's easy to write laws but hard to govern. It's the same as now — I ask you, Count — who'll run the departments when everyone has to pass examinations?"
"Those who pass the examinations, I suppose," replied Kochubey, crossing his legs and looking around.
"Well, I have Pryanichnikov serving under me — a splendid man, a priceless man — but he's sixty. Is he supposed to take an examination?"
"Yes, that's a difficulty, since education is not yet widespread, but..."

Count Kochubey didn't finish. He stood up, took Prince Andrew's arm, and went to meet a tall, bald, fair-haired man of about forty, with a large open forehead and a long face of unusual, peculiar whiteness, who was just entering. The newcomer wore a blue tailcoat with a cross on a ribbon around his neck and a star on his left breast. It was Speransky. Prince Andrew recognized him at once and felt a throb within him — as happens at critical moments of life. Whether it was respect, envy, or anticipation, he couldn't tell. Speransky's whole figure was of a distinctive type that made him instantly recognizable. In the society Prince Andrew frequented, he had never encountered anyone who combined such awkward, clumsy gestures with such calm self-possession; he had never seen such a resolute yet gentle expression as that in those half-closed, slightly moist eyes, or so firm a smile that expressed nothing in particular; nor had he heard such a refined, smooth, soft voice. Above all, he had never seen such delicate whiteness of face and hands — broad hands, but very plump, soft, and white. Such whiteness and softness Prince Andrew had only seen on the faces of soldiers who had been in the hospital a long time. This was Speransky, Secretary of State, the Emperor's constant companion and counselor at Erfurt, where he had met and talked with Napoleon on more than one occasion.

Speransky did not shift his gaze from face to face as people instinctively do when entering a large gathering, and was in no hurry to speak. He spoke slowly, confident he would be listened to, and looked only at the person he was addressing.

Prince Andrew followed Speransky's every word and gesture with particular attention. As sometimes happens — especially with people who judge those around them harshly — whenever he met someone new, especially someone he knew by reputation, like Speransky, he expected to discover in him the perfection of human qualities.

Speransky told Kochubey he was sorry he couldn't come sooner — he'd been held up at the palace. He didn't say the Emperor had detained him, and Prince Andrew noticed this affectation of modesty. When Kochubey introduced him, Speransky slowly turned his gaze to Bolkonski with his customary smile and looked at him in silence.
"I am very glad to make your acquaintance. I've heard of you, as everyone has," he said after a pause.
Kochubey said a few words about Arakcheev's reception of Bolkonski. Speransky smiled more noticeably.

"The chairman of the Army Regulations Committee is my good friend Monsieur Magnitsky," he said, fully articulating every word and syllable, "and if you like, I can put you in touch with him." He paused at the period. "I hope you will find him open-minded and ready to support everything reasonable."
A circle quickly formed around Speransky, and the old man who had talked about his subordinate Pryanichnikov addressed a question to him.

Prince Andrew, without joining the conversation, watched Speransky's every move — this man who not long ago had been an insignificant seminary student and now, Bolkonski thought, held in his plump white hands the fate of Russia. Prince Andrew was struck by the extraordinary disdainful composure with which Speransky answered the old man. He seemed to be addressing condescending words to him from an immeasurable height. When the old man started talking too loudly, Speransky smiled and said he couldn't judge the merits of what pleased the sovereign.
After chatting briefly in the general circle, Speransky rose and came up to Prince Andrew, taking him to the far end of the room. It was clear he thought it worth cultivating Bolkonski.

"I had no chance to talk with you, Prince, during that lively exchange the venerable gentleman drew me into," he said, with a slightly contemptuous smile that seemed to say: "You and I both understand how insignificant those people are." This flattered Prince Andrew. "I've known of you for some time — first from your liberation of your serfs, a pioneering example that deserves many more imitators, and second because you are one of those gentlemen of the chamber who have not taken offense at the new decree regarding court ranks, which is causing so much gossip and indignation."
"No," said Prince Andrew, "my father did not want me to take advantage of that privilege. I began my service from the lowest grade."
"Your father — a man of the previous century — evidently stands above our contemporaries who so condemn a measure that merely restores natural justice."

"I think, however, that these objections have some basis," said Prince Andrew, trying to resist Speransky's influence, which he was beginning to feel. He didn't want to agree with him on everything and felt a need to push back. Though he usually spoke easily and well, he found it hard to express himself now while talking with Speransky — he was too absorbed in studying the famous man's personality.
"Grounds of personal ambition, perhaps," Speransky said quietly.
"And of state interest, to some extent," said Prince Andrew.
"What do you mean?" asked Speransky softly, lowering his eyes.

"I am an admirer of Montesquieu," replied Prince Andrew, "and his idea that the principle of monarchies is honor strikes me as indisputable. Certain rights and privileges of the nobility seem to me a means of sustaining that sentiment."
"The principle of monarchies is honor seems to me incontestable. Certain rights and privileges for the aristocracy appear to me a means of maintaining that sentiment."
The smile vanished from Speransky's white face, which was much improved by the change. Apparently Prince Andrew's thought genuinely interested him.
"If you look at the question from that angle..." he began, pronouncing French with visible difficulty and speaking even more slowly than in Russian but quite calmly.
"If you regard the question from that point of view."

Speransky went on to say that honor — l'honneur — cannot be upheld by privileges that harm the state; that honor is either a negative concept of refraining from what is blameworthy, or it is a source of emulation in the pursuit of commendation and rewards. His arguments were concise, simple, and clear.

"An institution that upholds honor as a source of emulation — something like the Legion of Honor established by the great Emperor Napoleon — is not harmful but helpful to the success of the service, and is not a class or court privilege."

"I don't dispute that, but it cannot be denied that court privileges have served the same purpose," Prince Andrew responded. "Every courtier considers himself bound to maintain his position with dignity."

"Yet you yourself haven't chosen to avail yourself of the privilege, Prince," said Speransky, indicating by a smile that he wished to end amiably a discussion that was becoming uncomfortable for his companion. "If you would do me the honor of calling on Wednesday," he added, "I will have spoken with Magnitsky by then and can tell you what may interest you. I would also welcome the chance for a more extended conversation."
Closing his eyes, he gave a French-style bow without saying goodbye and, trying to draw as little attention as possible, left the room.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: During the first weeks of his stay in Petersburg, Prince Andrew felt the entire framework of thought he had built during his secluded country life overshadowed by the trivial demands that engulfed him in the city.

Returning home each evening, he would jot down four or five necessary calls or appointments in his notebook. The mechanics of daily life — arranging his schedule so as to be everywhere on time — absorbed most of his vital energy. He did nothing, didn't even think or find time to think, but only talked — and talked successfully — about what he had thought about while in the country.

He sometimes noticed with annoyance that he repeated the same remark on the same day in different circles. But he was so busy from morning to night that he had no time to notice he was thinking about nothing.

As at their first meeting at Kochubey's, Speransky made a powerful impression on Prince Andrew when he received him privately at his own house on Wednesday and talked to him at length and in confidence.

To Bolkonski, so many people seemed contemptible and insignificant, and he so longed to find in someone the living ideal of perfection toward which he strived, that he readily believed he had found this ideal in Speransky — a perfectly rational and virtuous man. Had Speransky come from the same class and had the same breeding and traditions, Bolkonski would quickly have discovered his weak, human, unheroic sides. But Speransky's strange, logical turn of mind inspired a respect that was all the greater because he didn't fully understand the man. Moreover, Speransky — whether because he genuinely appreciated the other's abilities or because he considered it necessary to win him over — showed off his dispassionate, calm rationality before Prince Andrew and flattered him with that subtle flattery that goes hand in hand with self-confidence: the tacit assumption that one's companion is the only other person besides oneself capable of seeing the foolishness of the rest of mankind and the reasonableness of one's own ideas.

During their long conversation on Wednesday evening, Speransky said more than once: "We look at everything that rises above the common level of established custom..." or, with a smile: "But we want the wolves fed and the sheep safe..." or: "They can't understand this..." — all in a way that seemed to say: "We — you and I — understand what they are and who we are."

This first long conversation with Speransky only deepened in Prince Andrew the feeling he had had at their first encounter. He saw in him a remarkable, clear-thinking man of vast intellect who, through energy and persistence, had attained power — and who was using it solely for Russia's good. In Prince Andrew's eyes, Speransky was the man he himself would have wished to be: one who could account rationally for every fact of life, who considered only what was rational to be important, and who could apply the standard of reason to everything. Everything seemed so simple and clear in Speransky's presentation that Prince Andrew found himself agreeing on every point. If he argued back, it was only to maintain his independence and not submit to Speransky's views entirely. Everything was right and as it should be — with one exception that troubled Prince Andrew: Speransky's cold, mirrorlike gaze, which didn't let you see into his soul, and his delicate white hands, which Prince Andrew kept watching involuntarily, the way one watches the hands of those who hold power. That mirrorlike look and those soft hands irritated Prince Andrew, though he didn't know why. He was also unpleasantly struck by the excessive contempt for others he observed in Speransky, and by the variety of logical maneuvers he used to support his positions. He deployed every kind of mental tool except analogy, and shifted too boldly, Prince Andrew felt, from one mode to another. At one moment he would take the stance of a practical man and dismiss dreamers; then he would become a satirist, laughing ironically at his opponents; then he would grow severely logical; then suddenly soar into the realm of metaphysics. (This last tactic he used very frequently.) He would elevate a question to metaphysical heights, jump to definitions of space, time, and thought, and having extracted the rebuttal he needed, would descend again to the original level of discussion.

In general, what struck Prince Andrew most about Speransky's mind was his absolute, unshakable faith in the power and authority of reason. It was clear that the thought which to Prince Andrew seemed so natural — namely, that everything one thinks and believes might ultimately be nonsense — could never occur to Speransky. And it was precisely this trait that especially attracted Prince Andrew.

During the first period of their acquaintance, Bolkonski felt a passionate admiration for Speransky similar to what he had once felt for Bonaparte. The fact that Speransky was the son of a village priest, and that petty people might despise him for his humble origins (as many did), only made Prince Andrew cherish this feeling more and unconsciously reinforce it.

That first evening, Bolkonski mentioned the Commission for the Revision of the Legal Code. Speransky told him sardonically that the Commission had existed for 150 years, had cost millions, and had accomplished nothing — except that Rosenkampf had stuck labels on the corresponding paragraphs of the different codes.

"And that is all the state has to show for the millions it spent," he said. "We want to give the Senate new judicial powers, but we have no laws. That is why it's a sin for men like you, Prince, not to be serving in times like these!"
Prince Andrew said that such work required a legal education he did not have.
"But nobody has it, so what would you have? It's a vicious circle, and we must break out of it."

A week later, Prince Andrew was a member of the Committee on Army Regulations and — what he hadn't expected at all — chairman of a section of the commission for revising the legal code. At Speransky's request, he took on the first part of the Civil Code being drafted and, using the Napoleonic Code and the Institutes of Justinian, began working on the section on Personal Rights.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: Nearly two years earlier, in 1808, Pierre had returned to Petersburg from his estates and found himself involuntarily thrust into a leading role among the city's Freemasons. He organized dinner meetings and funeral lodge gatherings, enrolled new members, and worked to unite various lodges and obtain authentic charters. He donated money for the construction of temples and made up the shortfall in charitable contributions, which most members were stingy and irregular about paying. He almost single-handedly supported a poorhouse the Order had founded in Petersburg.

His own life, meanwhile, continued as before — the same indulgences and dissipations. He liked to eat and drink well, and though he considered it immoral and degrading, he could not resist the temptations of the bachelor circles in which he moved.

Amid the whirl of his activities and distractions, however, Pierre began to feel — by the end of a year — that the more firmly he tried to stand on the ground of Masonry, the more it gave way beneath him. At the same time, he felt that the deeper it sank, the more inextricably bound he became to the Order. When he first joined the Freemasons, he had felt like a man confidently stepping onto what looks like the smooth surface of a bog. When he put one foot down, it sank. To make sure of the ground, he put the other foot down — and sank deeper. And now he was stuck, wading knee-deep in the mire whether he liked it or not.

Joseph Alexeevich was not in Petersburg — he had lately withdrawn from the affairs of the Petersburg lodges and lived almost entirely in Moscow. All the lodge members were men Pierre knew in ordinary life, and it was hard for him to see them merely as Brothers in Freemasonry rather than as Prince B. or Ivan Vasilevich D., whom he knew socially as weak and unimpressive men. Beneath the Masonic aprons and insignia, he saw the mundane uniforms and medals they coveted in real life. Often, after collecting dues and tallying the twenty or thirty rubles received — mostly in promises — from a dozen members, half of whom could pay as easily as he could, Pierre remembered the Masonic vow in which each Brother pledged to devote all his worldly goods to his neighbor. Doubts he tried to suppress kept rising in his soul.

He divided the Brothers he knew into four categories. In the first he placed those who took no active part in the affairs of the lodges or in the world, but were exclusively occupied with the mystical science of the Order — questions about the threefold name of God, the three primordial elements (sulphur, mercury, and salt), or the meaning of the square and the various symbols of Solomon's temple. Pierre respected this class — to which the senior members mostly belonged, including, he believed, Joseph Alexeevich himself — but he didn't share their interests. His heart wasn't in the mystical side of Freemasonry.
In the second category he placed himself and others like him — seekers and doubters who hadn't yet found a clear, direct path in Freemasonry but hoped to.

In the third he put those Brothers (the majority) who saw nothing in Freemasonry but its outward forms and ceremonies and valued their strict performance without caring about their meaning or purpose. Willarski and even the Grand Master of the principal lodge belonged to this group.

Finally, the fourth category — also very large — consisted of men who believed in nothing and wanted nothing, but joined the Freemasons simply to associate with the wealthy young brothers who were influential through their connections or rank, and of whom there were a great many in the lodge.

Pierre began to feel dissatisfied with what he was doing. Freemasonry — at least as he experienced it — sometimes seemed to him based on nothing but outward show. He didn't dream of doubting Freemasonry itself, but suspected that Russian Masonry had taken a wrong turn and departed from its original principles. And so, toward the end of the year, he went abroad to be initiated into the Order's higher mysteries.

In the summer of 1809, Pierre returned to Petersburg. The Russian Freemasons, who had learned through correspondence with their foreign counterparts that Bezukhov had gained the trust of many highly placed individuals, had been initiated into numerous secrets, had been elevated to a higher degree, and was bringing back much that could benefit the Masonic cause in Russia — all came to see him, tried to win his favor, and seemed to believe he was preparing something for them while keeping it to himself.

A solemn meeting of the second-degree lodge was convened, at which Pierre promised to share with the Petersburg Brothers what he had been charged to deliver from the Order's highest leaders. The hall was full. After the customary rituals, Pierre stood and began his address.

"Dear Brothers," he began, blushing and stammering, a written speech in his hand, "it is not enough to observe our mysteries in the seclusion of our lodge — we must act — act! We are asleep, but we must act." Pierre raised his notebook and began to read.

"For the spread of pure truth and the triumph of virtue," he read, "we must cleanse men of prejudice, promote principles in harmony with the spirit of the times, undertake the education of the young, unite ourselves in unbreakable bonds with the wisest men, and boldly yet prudently combat superstition, unbelief, and folly, forming from those devoted to us a body linked by common purpose and possessing authority and power.

"To this end, we must secure the dominance of virtue over vice and strive to ensure that the honest man may, even in this world, receive a lasting reward for his goodness. But in these great efforts we are gravely hampered by the political institutions of today. What is to be done? Favor revolutions? Overthrow everything? Repel force by force? No! We are far from that. Every violent reform deserves condemnation, for it cannot remedy evil while men remain what they are, and because wisdom has no need of violence.

"The entire plan of our Order should be grounded in the idea of cultivating men of strength and virtue, bound by shared conviction, whose purpose is to punish vice and folly, patronize talent and goodness, and raise worthy men from obscurity into our Brotherhood. Only then will our Order have the power to quietly restrain the supporters of disorder and control them without their even knowing it. In a word, we must establish a form of government with universal reach, spread across the whole world, without dissolving the bonds of citizenship — one alongside which all other governments can continue as usual in everything except what impedes the great aim of our Order: to secure the victory of virtue over vice. This was Christianity's own aim. It taught men to be wise and good and, for their own benefit, to follow the example and instruction of the best and wisest men.

"In those times, when everything was plunged in darkness, preaching alone was naturally enough. The novelty of Truth gave her special power. But now we need far stronger methods. It is now necessary that man, governed by his senses, should find in virtue something tangible and attractive to those senses. It is impossible to uproot the passions; but we must strive to direct them toward noble ends, and therefore everyone must be able to satisfy his passions within the bounds of virtue. Our Order should provide the means for this.

"As soon as we have a certain number of worthy men in every country, each training two others, all closely united — everything will be possible for our Order, which has already accomplished much in secret for the good of mankind."

This speech not only made a strong impression but caused a stir in the lodge. The majority of Brothers, seeing in it the dangerous ideas of Illuminism, received it with a coldness that surprised Pierre. The Grand Master began to reply, and Pierre defended his views with growing passion. It had been a long time since there had been so heated a meeting. Factions formed — some accusing Pierre of Illuminism, others supporting him. At that meeting, Pierre was struck for the first time by the infinite variety of human minds, which makes it impossible for a truth to present itself the same way to any two people. Even those who seemed to be on his side understood him in their own way, with reservations and modifications he couldn't accept — since what he wanted most of all was to convey his thoughts to others exactly as he understood them himself.
The Illuminati sought to replace monarchical institutions with republican ones.

At the end of the meeting, the Grand Master rebuked Bezukhov — with irony and ill will — for his vehemence, saying it was not only a love of virtue but also a love of argument that had driven him. Pierre did not respond, and asked simply whether his proposal would be accepted. He was told it would not. Without waiting for the usual formalities, he left the lodge and went home.
